The United States announced tougher export controls on AI chips on Monday after a scandal involving Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang exposed a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies. The news came the day before Californian chip titan Nvidia reports its first earnings since Huang’s departure as CEO, with investors questioning if the artificial intelligence boom can hold strong. Under Washington’s new rules, data centres anywhere in the world will need a US license to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes. The rules also require licenses to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, countries the US Commerce Department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips. These changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in Southeast Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China. While this loophole has been known to authorities, the revelation of Nvidia co-founder Huang’s extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice. The woman, Alice Huang, is a former executive of Megaspeed — a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in violation of export controls. Jensen Huang, 63, stepped down last week after at least two extramarital affairs were revealed in media reports. Facing criticism, the US Commerce Department said Monday it would close a loophole that had drawn concern from US authorities. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Add us to your Preferred Sources The move “is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries,” the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement. It weighed on Nvidia’s shares, which shed four percent on Monday, extending a slide since the scandal erupted. • ‘Business-as-usual’ unlikely – Nvidia stock has lost more than a quarter of its value over the past month, as doubts grow about the health of the AI investment boom. Tuesday’s results will be the first presented under chief financial officer, Colette Kress, who is serving as interim CEO. “If they try to keep a business-as-usual tone in the call, I think that it probably wouldn’t be well received,” said Jacob Bourne of Emarketer, describing the company as in turmoil. Investors will be watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang’s aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies. Analysts said they would also be eyeing Nvidia’s guidance on future sales, along with its chip sales in Asia, particularly Singapore. That could ripple across the AI investments propping up the US economy — with Nvidia backing major labs including Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, which is expected to begin trading on Wall Street on Thursday. Tech firms dragged Asian stock markets down again Tuesday as the fallout from the Nvidia crisis rattles trading floors, with the new US moves on chip controls adding to uncertainty. • ‘Trusted access’ – On Tuesday, Singapore said it was engaging with affected companies and talking to US authorities to ascertain the scope and implementation of the new measures. The city-state is also “exploring how to facilitate trusted access (to AI chips) for Singapore companies”, a government statement said. Indonesia said it was reviewing the measure “and seeking industry input on its potential impact on operations and investment, including in the data centre sector”. The scandal has exposed a rift within the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for an investigation into Jensen Huang’s dealings with Megaspeed, and accuses the Commerce Department of ignoring widespread reports that Megaspeed was shifting Nvidia technology to China. Tech tycoon Elon Musk and other major AI investors are meanwhile gathering signatures for an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement. “The most important time to help someone is when they’re down,” investor Bill Ackman said at a Semafor tech conference. Before leaving for summits in Asia, President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang back at Nvidia, waving off the security concerns. But given the legal cloud over him, most Wall Street analysts doubt that the AI rock star can return anytime soon. Kress, a non-engineer, is not expected to stay in the role permanently, leaving Nvidia facing a high-stakes search for a successor. AFP Kindly share this story:
